**DATASCI 406 FA 26, Quiz 1.4**

**Name and Uniqname:**

## Question 1 (1 point)

You simulate $B = 999$ datasets under $H_0$ and find that **every** simulated
value of the test statistic is smaller than the observed $t_{\text{obs}}$.
What do you report? **Circle one.**

1. $\hat p = 0$
1. $\hat p = 1/1000$
1. $\hat p = 1/999$
1. $\hat p < 0.05$; the simulation cannot pin the value down any further.

### Solution

**Answer: 2.** $\hat p = (1 + \#\{T_b \ge t_{\text{obs}}\})/(B + 1)$ counts the
observed statistic among the draws. It can never return 0, and it makes the
test exactly valid rather than approximately so. Option 1 calls the data
impossible under $H_0$ when we only failed to simulate enough; option 3 has
the right idea and the wrong denominator.

## Question 2 (1 point)

$X_1, \ldots, X_{25}$ are independent draws from $N(\mu, 1)$; the statistic $T$
is the **sample median**; $H_0 : \mu = 0$ against $H_1 : \mu = 0.35$; and the
rejection region was fixed in advance as $T > 0.3$.

```{r echo = TRUE}
set.seed(406)
null <- replicate(20000, median(rnorm(25, 0.00, 1)))
alt  <- replicate(20000, median(rnorm(25, 0.35, 1)))
round(c(A = mean(alt),      B = mean(null > 0.3),
        C = mean(alt < 0.3), D = mean(alt > 0.3)), 3)
```

Which printed value is the **size** of this test, and which is its **power**
against $\mu = 0.35$? Write one label in each blank.

size $=$ \underline{\hspace{0.5in}} \qquad power $=$ \underline{\hspace{0.5in}}

### Solution

**size $=$ `B` (0.116), power $=$ `D` (0.580).**

Both average the same indicator, $T > 0.3$. They differ only in which world
made the data: `null` under $H_0$, `alt` under $H_1$. Read the error table
down a column.

- `C` $= 0.420$ is $\beta$ --- the power's world, counting the failures
  ($0.420 + 0.580 = 1$).
- `A` $= 0.352$ averages the **statistic**, not an indicator. It estimates the
  alternative's median: a fact about the data, not about the test.

The size is 0.116, not 0.05. The cutoff was fixed first, so the size is
whatever it delivers. Resize with `quantile(null, 0.95)` $= 0.408$ and the
power falls to 0.41 --- which is why power only compares at a common size.

**Rubric.** 1 pt for both blanks; no partial credit.

## Question 3 (3 points)

$X_1, \ldots, X_{40}$ are independent $\text{Exp}(\text{rate} = \theta)$ with
$\theta$ unknown. The test statistic is the 25% trimmed mean
`mean(x, trim = 0.25)`, which has no convenient sampling distribution. The
observed data give $t_{\text{obs}} = 1.39$.

Suppose we have implemented a **two-sided level-0.05 test** of $H_0 : \theta = \theta_0$ against
$H_1 : \theta \ne \theta_0$, for one particular $\theta_0$ using a Monte Carlo hypothesis test.
The procedure is implemented as a function `test(t_obs, theta_0)` that returns
`TRUE` if the hypothesis is rejected and `FALSE` if the hypothesis is not
rejected.

Using this function, describe how you would
produce a **95% confidence interval for $\theta$**. Your answer must say both
(i) what you would compute, in enough detail that someone could code it from
your description, and (ii) why what you get is a 95% interval. You may suppose that $\theta$ is known to fall in some range $[a,b]$.

<!-- answer-space: 2.5in -->

### Solution

**(i)** Hold the data fixed, so `t_obs` never changes, and call `test()` at
every candidate $\theta_0$ across $[a, b]$. Keep the ones it does **not**
reject; that set is the interval.

```{r echo = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
grid <- seq(a, b, by = 0.005)
reject <- map_lgl(grid, function(th) test(t_obs, th))
range(grid[!reject])
```

One point for the sweep, one point for keeping values where function returns FALSE.

**(ii)** Let $\theta$ be the true value. The test has level 0.05, so handed
the true null it returns `TRUE` with probability 0.05. The kept set is exactly
where it returned `FALSE`, so it contains $\theta$ with probability 0.95. Therefore it is a proper 95% CI.

No credit for restating how the test works in place of a coverage argument.

One point for correct justification.
